title: xDSL: Sidekick Compilation for SSA-Based Compilers
problem: Compiler researchers face trade-offs: prototyping in production compilers is cumbersome (optimized for speed over simplicity), while new prototype compilers require significant engineering to transition to production.
motivation: Bridging prototype and production compilation enables faster development cycles for compiler research while leveraging production-ready infrastructure for deployment.
method: Instead of forcing researchers to choose between working inside a production compiler (messy but useful) or building their own from scratch (clean but too much work), this approach creates multiple specialized compilers that work together. They share the same text format for describing code structure (called IR, or intermediate representation) and use a declarative system called IRDL to define how each compiler's extensions work, so each one can focus on what it does best—prototyping, teaching, or production use—while still sharing code with others. The paper demonstrates this with xDSL, a specialized compiler that works alongside MLIR (an existing production framework) and can exchange code with it because they use the same textual IR.
key_novelty: This is the first system that lets multiple specialized compilers—each optimized for different purposes like prototyping, teaching, or production—work together by sharing code in the same text format and using declarative rules to define their extensions.
contributions: Sidekick compiler framework concept for prototyping-to-production workflow
xDSL as MLIR sidekick for teaching and research
Shared textual IR and IRDL dialect for framework exchange
Demonstration on three use cases: teaching, DSL compilation, rewrite systems
limitations: Trade-offs in performance or optimization coverage between frameworks not quantified.
